ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: “When hungry, eat rice” recurs as an answer and self-description, while Dazhu Huihai explicitly distinguishes his eating from the distracted eating attributed to other people.
EvidenceBody: When hunger comes, eat rice. Zen records turn the ordinary act into a compact answer, self-description, quotation, and point of public criticism, usually paired with sleeping when tired. Huanglong Huinan places it in a four-action series after contrasting ways of seeing a staff: eat when hungry, sleep when tired, approach fire when cold, and take coolness when hot . Dahui Zonggao quotes Lingzhao's reply, neither hard nor easy—when hungry, eat rice; when tired, sleep , and appraises the Pang family as walking together but not in step. Yuanwu Keqin uses the graphic variant ‘when hungry, eat rice’ beside ordinary mind. Dongshan Zhiqian uses that variant in his own self-description, saying that he does not know how to discuss Chan or speak of the Way and only eats when hungry and sleeps when tired. Dazhu Huihai supplies the explicit contrast: other people refuse simply to eat or sleep and instead make a hundred demands and a thousand calculations. Hongzhi Zhengjue also refuses the line as a sufficient slogan: the monastery manager knows only eating when hungry and does not know the many kinds of affairs . The ordinary meal is therefore bent into interview language, but the records themselves prevent merely repeating it from settling the matter.
